questions.q: What is the most common mistake new consultants make in the first 30 days, according to this lesson?
options: Asking too many clarifying questions about the client's environment
Trying to "fix" something before understanding why the client's environment is set up that way
Spending too much time reading the client's existing documentation
Shadowing the close process too closely
questions.explain: A real client's instance has its own configuration history and reasons behind its setup. Jumping in to fix something before understanding why it's configured that way is the common first-30-days mistake.

questions.q: By roughly day 60, what kind of work should a new consultant realistically be taking on?
options: Only observing, with no real tasks assigned at all
Unreviewed, unlimited scope changes to production with no oversight
Real tasks and tickets within a scope someone more senior still reviews before it goes live
Complete ownership of the entire client relationship
questions.explain: By day 60, a realistic goal is contributing real, well-bounded work that is still reviewed by someone more senior before going live.

questions.q: What does this lesson say trust is built on most, between days 61 and 90?
options: Communication - flagging problems early, giving realistic timelines, and documenting clearly - more than technical correctness alone
Working exclusively alone with no communication at all
Avoiding any conversation about problems until they resolve themselves
Technical correctness alone, regardless of communication
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that trust at this stage comes less from pure technical correctness and more from communication: early flags, realistic timelines, and clear documentation.

questions.q: What mistake does the lesson specifically warn against during the days 61-90 window?
options: Owning a defined piece of work end to end
Going quiet when something is wrong instead of raising it
Documenting work clearly enough for someone else to pick up
Giving a realistic timeline instead of an optimistic one
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against going silent when something is wrong - the opposite of the communication habits it recommends building.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say it's credible, not weak, to admit the capstone doesn't fully replace real client experience?
options: Because the capstone experience is completely irrelevant to a real consulting role
Because it is dishonest to ever mention training experience in a professional setting
Because an honest acknowledgment of the capstone's real value and its real limits is a mature, credible answer that builds confidence rather than undermining it
Because admitting any limitation always destroys credibility immediately
questions.explain: The lesson frames honest self-assessment - naming what the capstone really gave you and what it didn't - as a mature, credible answer, not a weakness.
